## Probing Muon + b-Jet Resonances in pp Collisions with the ATLAS Detector

Abstract

Probing heavy resonances in collider physics has been a longstanding and fruitful endeavor. De-

spite well-motivated candidates like leptoquarks and their role in grand unified theories, direct experi-

mental searches for lepton–quark resonances in proton–proton collisions are relatively scarce. Cross-

generational lepton–quark resonances have received even less experimental attention. This thesis

presents an ATLAS search for one such under-represented resonance: the muon and b-jet resonance.

The search leverages the full Run 2 and partial Run 3 datasets at √s = 13 TeV and √s = 13.6 TeV,

respectively. For a measure of sensitivity, a benchmark leptoquark ˜S1 model with only muon and b-

quark Yukawa couplings is used. Using the CLs statistical method, the analysis improves upon prior

leptoquark mass exclusion limits for couplings above ∼1.

## Introduction

The Higgs boson discovery in 2012 by the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) experiments ATLAS and

CMS was hailed as a confirmation of the Higgs mechanism [1, 2]. As such, it was also a confirma-

tion of the highest-energy dynamical phenomenological property of the Standard Model (SM) of

particle physics. Energy scales at, and immediately above, the electroweak symmetry breaking scale

O(100 GeV) have been thoroughly explored by a range of ATLAS measurements since [3–6]. No

smoking gun signatures hinting at any beyond the standard model (BSM) properties have been ob-

served.

LHCcollisionsprobehigh-energyphenomenabycollidingprotonswithultra-relativisticmomenta.

1


<!-- Page 21 -->


The duality of momentum and distance inherent to quantum theories can be invoked to claim that

LHC collisions probe the smallest distance scales ever probed by measurements. The 100 GeV elec-

troweak scale converts to ∼10−18 m. Pushing the analogy one step further, the LHC experiments

can be viewed as the world’s most powerful microscopes. Or at least the world’s most powerful micro-

scopes with a steady and lab-controlled “light source” (collision source). Although there is no guaran-

tee of seeing new emergent phenomena, energy frontier particle physics measurements keep probing

smaller and smaller length scales.

As opposed to optical microscopes, collider experiments like ATLAS do not, on their own, provide

a complete picture of interactions at the 10−18 m length scale. This is because new phenomenologi-

cal features could in principle lie in any corner of phase space, while measurements at ATLAS target

specific signatures. Up until the Higgs discovery (and largely also since then) theories promising “nat-

uralness” have guided and motivated the search for particular signatures in particle physics to great

avail [7]. However, it has also been argued that the naturalness paradigm has run its course and that

new approaches should be explored [8].

The motivation for the analysis presented in this thesis is derived from a layered deconstruction of

the naturalness-inspired approach. The presented measurement is not designed to probe any partic-

ular high-energy completion to the SM, but does target an invariant mass resonance.

Many resonant final states have been part of the canon of ATLAS and CMS measurements. How-

ever, there has generally been a focus on probing resonances with SM-like counterparts: such as Z′

and W ′ resonances that directly couple quarks to quarks or leptons to leptons. Furthermore, many

resonant searches have focused on same-flavor, or same-generation signatures. So far, searches for res-

onances that do not have SM counterparts have been probed less. For a holistic “picture” of 10−18 m

scale interactions, a probe of these less conventional resonances is motivated.

## 2

## Leptoquarks

Leptoquarks (LQs) are a proposed beyond the standard model (BSM) particle. Their defining feature

is their direct coupling to both quarks and leptons – this feature contrasts all standard model (SM)

particles. Interest in LQs was born from naturalness-driven proposals to unify SM lie groups, merg-

ing particle representations. In 1973 J. Pati and A. Salam presented LQs as byproducts of “matter

unification” [10]. Matter unification refers to the general concept that at some energy scale all massive

fermions may be grouped into a single representation of some higher symmetry group. Any gauge

unified theory featuring multiplets that mix quarks and leptons is guaranteed to give birth to LQs at

the energy scale where the higher symmetry is broken. As a result, LQs are an inescapable feature for

5


<!-- Page 25 -->


any gauge unified theory that also attempts to unify the SM fermions.

Although the naturalness appeal of LQs stems from their prominent role in unification, they are

generally defined in a bottom-up approach. Any particle that A) couples quarks and leptons directly,

B) respects all SM gauge symmetries, and C) is renormalizable can be considered a LQ. Despite such

loose requirements, only 12 LQs with distinct quantum numbers can satisfy these conditions [11].

Although each LQ features a wealth of tunable yukawa couplings, they remain especially simple to

categorize.

There have been a wealth of LQ searches ever since their conception. These searches fall into two

broad categories. There are indirect and direct searches. Indirect searches rely on probing the low-

energy effects of a LQ. This generally involves extracting effective field theory (EFT) 4-fermi Wilson

coefficients from LQ models, and expressing them in terms of LQ mass and couplings. Measuring

branching fractions in leptonic hadron decays is the most common method for constraining these

Wilson coefficients, however, many other low-energy phenomena have also been used. These searches

are considered indirect since they probe the low-energy features of LQs, however, they cannot show

conclusively that a true LQ is responsible for the low-energy effects. In contrast, direct searches look

across the full energy spectrum of LQ phenomenology. This involves facilitating LQ production near

its on-shell energy threshold, and then reconstructing the LQ’s invariant mass spectrum to identify a

resonance. This approach lends itself to collider based physics. The analysis presented in this thesis is

a direct LQ search.

number that differentiates LQs. Any given LQ’s hypercharge must exactly cancel the hypercharge of

the quark-lepton pair it couples to. Mixing and matching all possible combinations of quarks and

leptons doubles the number of distinct LQs for a final count of 12 distinct LQs, 6 scalar and 6 vector.

## Large Hadron Collider

The ATLAS detector is installed in the point one (P1) cavern of the LHC tunnel – it is one of just four

experiments situated at the four interaction points of the LHC. Since the LHC is the world’s largest

particle accelerator, producing the world’s highest energy proton-proton (and heavy-ion) collisions,

ATLAS and the other LHC experiments have a unique role in the high energy frontier of particle

physics.

The LHC employs super-conducting magnets to accelerate protons (in both directions) around

an underground tunnel 27 km in circumference [31]. The proton beams are focused and bent to

yield proton collisions at the four interaction points of the LHC. Since the LHC’s Run 3 operat-

ing period (beginning in 2022), the LHC has been colliding protons at a center-of-mass energy of √s = 13.6 TeV. For the Run 2 data-taking period (2015-2018), the LHC produced proton-proton

collisions at √s = 13 TeV. Protons are clustered in bunches, and therefore the proton collisions oc-

cur at regular intervals dubbed bunch crossings, that occur every 25ns, or 40 million times per second.

3.1 Acceleration

The entire accelerator chain relies on applying electromagnetic fields to accelerate, guide, and focus

beams of charged particles. There are three principle components to this:

• Radiofrequency (RF) cavities: A metallic chamber within which electromagnetic fields can be

oscillated at very high frequencies. The field oscillations are synchronized such that the electric

field points toward the center of the cavity with an approaching bunch of positively charged

hadrons, pulling them along. Once the proton bunch passes the center of the RF cavity the

fields reverse direction, now pointing away from the center of the cavity, pushing the bunch

along.

• Dipole magnets: These superconducting magnets apply a magnetic field perpendicular to the

beam axis, as well as the earth’s horizontal plane. This bends the beam, guiding it.

• Quadrupole magnets: These superconducting magnets apply a magnetic field as shown in fig-

ure 3.1. These magnets are employed to squeeze the beam. These magnets are used to prepare

the beam, keep it from degrading, as well as focus it for collisions.

Magnets used to guide, accelerate and maintain the beam (mostly dipoles and quadrupoles) are

referred to as lattice magnets. Magnets used to focus the beam for collisions (quadrupoles) are referred

to as insertion magnets.

3.3 Pileup

The utility of integrated luminosity is in its power to predict an expected number of events given a the-

## ATLAS Detector

The ATLAS detector is designed to observe the spray of remnants from hadron collisions. These

remnants can include all semi-stable SM particles. To detect, and measure properties of as many of

these particles as possible, the ATLAS detector features multiple subsystems, each specialized for a

particular purpose. The 25 ns bunch crossings delivered by the LHC require ATLAS to have excellent

temporal resolution and subsystem inter-calibration. The ATLAS detector is exceptionally complex,

this chapter will provide only a high-level overview of the most relevant features relating to the analysis

presented in this thesis.

4.1 Coordinate System

The overall cylindrical shape of the ATLAS detector is reflective of the axial symmetry of the proton

and heavy-ion collisions at the interaction point. As such, aligning the z-axis with the beam axis,

symmetry across the z = 0 plane, the sign convention of z is generally not of great importance in

4.2 Magnets

Although the tracking detectors in ATLAS could independently determine the direction of momen-

tum of charged particles, alone they would have no sensitivity to a high energy particle’s momentum.

It is the magnetic fields in ATLAS that enable momentum measurements of tracks by bending the

trajectories of charged particles. The strength of the magnetic field, together with the curvature of the

tracks constrain the momentum of the particle that left the track. These momentum measurements

are described in more detail in section 5.1.

ATLAS employs two types of magnets. The superconducting solenoid magnet, and a set of super-

conducting toroidal magnets [38].

4.2.1 Solenoid Magnet

(the interaction point). The magnetic field at the center points along the beam axis. This choice is

optimal to maximally deflect particles with large transverse momentum, while preserving axial sym-

metry. Note, the orientation of the solenoid does break the ±ˆz symmetry of the detector.

The magnetic field is not constant throughout the inner detector. The magnetic field at z = 1.7m

is ∼1.8 T, and this falls to ∼0.9 T at the end of the inner detector cavity. Figure 4.3 shows a few

4.3 Sensor Technologies

Before delving into the details of the specific detector subsystems employed by ATLAS, it is worth

introducing the principles by which various ATLAS detector subsystems function. There are two

overall principles used to detect particles in ATLAS: ionization chambers, and scintillating counters.

4.3.1 Ionization Chambers

Most of the ATLAS detectors are ionization chambers: they work on the principle that when a par-

ticle traverses the active volume, it causes ionization of the material in the active volume. An electric

field applied across the active volume ensures that the charge carriers – be they electrons, ions, or holes

– drift toward the electrodes. The drifting charges induce a current for a short period of time. This

registers as a pulse, which can be amplified and shaped. Some ionization chamber detectors essentially

count hits, meaning that if a pulse passes a certain threshold, a hit is counted. Other ionization cham-

bers actually analyze the shape and size of the pulse to infer further properties of the ionizing particle.

The pulse is processed into digital data by front-end electronics that are placed on the detector. The

digital data is sent by fiber-optic cables to be interpreted further by dedicated computers. It is worth

noting that the drift-time of the charge effectively determines the width of the pulse, and as such, the

temporal resolution of the detector. For this reason, drift times must be around, or below, 25 ns to

ensure the detector can resolve one bunch crossing from the next2.

Therearemultiplechoicesfortheactivematerialintheionizationchambers. ThroughoutATLAS,

gaseous, liquid, and solid active materials are used.

In the case of gases and liquids, electrons and positively charged ions drift toward the electrodes.

Often, methods are employed to amplify the signal within the active material. For instance, thin wires

are often used as electrodes to increase the electric field strength near them. This accelerates drifting

2Workarounds exist for slightly larger drift times.

35


<!-- Page 55 -->


electrons to high enough energy to ionize other atoms in the material. This process can result in a

cascade of ionization that is easier to detect.

In the case of solid materials, doped semiconductors are used, such that electrons, and positively

charged holes drift toward the electrodes. Conducting materials would not be useful as any electric

field would in fact induce a dominant passive current. It turns out there is an optimal band gap for

the detector use-case. A band-gap that is sufficiently small to allow for abundant ionization due to

incident particles, but not too small, as to avoid thermal fluctuations from drowning the signal in

noise. Doping semi-conductors gives flexibility to effectively regulate this trade-off, by impeding the

flowofcurrent. Inparticular, npjunctionsinareverse-biasconfigurationwiththeappropriatevoltage

applied can tune the depletion zone to the sweet spot of picking up signal, and rejecting noise.

4.3.2 Scintillating Counters

The other detection principle relies on scintillation. When particles pass through a scintillator, in-

stead of ionizing the material, they often excite atoms. These excited states are quick to decay back

to the ground state, emitting light in the process. This emitted light can then be directed to a photo-

multiplier. The light hits the photo-multiplier tube’s photo-cathodes, which emit electrons. These

electrons can be guided, and accelerated toward a dynode. Upon reaching the dynode each electron

carries sufficient energy to free more electrons. A series of dynodes repeat this process, until suffi-

ciently many electrons are freed to form a detectable current. Just like for the ionization chambers,

an incident particle will therefore register as a pulse which can be shaped, processed, and digitized by

dedicated front-end electronics.

4.5 Calorimeters

After particles traverse the ID, they pass through the solenoid, and then encounter the calorimeter

system. The ID trackers were designed to reconstruct the tracks of particles, while keeping a low

material budget to prevent scattering and stopping. The calorimeter, in this sense, does the opposite.

It is designed to stop particles, and in so doing measure the energy the incident particle deposited

throughout the calorimeter.

The principle of a calorimeter relies on having slices of a suitable absorber material, and sensor ma-

terial. The absorber material should cause the incident particles to shower, and absorb the bulk of

the energy of the shower. The sensor material, which should be interleaved with sufficient density,

should allow the detector to read out an electric signal based on the size of the shower. Throughout

the ATLAS calorimeters, two technologies are used to read out the energy of the shower: liquid ar-

gon ionization chambers and scintillators (as described in section 4.3). When it comes to the absorber

material, there are two key material properties to keep in mind: radiation length X0 and nuclear in-

teraction length λn.

The electron radiation length X0 describes what length of the given material is needed to cause

an electron to brem down to 1/e of its original energy. Note, this describes only the energy loss due

to bremsstrahlung, however for high energy electrons this is a good approximation. It turns out that

high energy photons traversing material evolve mostly by creating electron-positron pairs, and that

4.6 Muon Spectrometer

Although the calorimeters stop electrons, photons, and hadrons (charged and neutral), muons gen-

erally pass through the calorimeters. This is because A) as leptons they do not participate in hadronic

Therefore, to ensure ATLAS doesn’t lose track of muons, another tracker system is needed to mea-

4.7 Triggers

The full ATLAS readout for a single event is of the order of a MB. If ATLAS tried to record every

bunch-crossing (40 MHz), it would amount to roughly 40TB every second. This is an intractable

amount of data to record, and process. However, this is slightly beside the point. The research fron-

tier that ATLAS measurements target relies on observing only rare, and high-energy events. ATLAS

48


<!-- Page 68 -->


triggers are designed as the first, live-time selection of potentially interesting events, and they save an-

alyzers the trouble of processing a large number of uninteresting events.

The goal of the ATLAS triggers [48–50] is to reduce the event rate from 40 MHz to an average

of 1.2 kHz (3 kHz) for Run 2 (Run 3). This event-rate amounts to a few GB/s. This is still a lot

of data, but is manageable. The triggers need to make a selection decision very quickly, and as such

the full readout of ATLAS is not used in this process. Instead, the detectors that are designed to

trigger (calorimeters and muon spectrometer) provide a quicker, lower-resolution output stream for

the trigger. The read-out is buffered while the trigger decision is made. Once a decision is made, the

full event is recorded, or discarded, accordingly.

After the detector-specific trigger data stream, which often include low latency reconstruction and

coincidence requirements, the trigger system is separated in two layers. First comes the Level-1 (L1)

trigger, which reduces the 40MHz rate down to 100 kHz. If the L1 trigger selects an event, a Level-1

Accept (L1A) is sent to the detector readout buffer, and a region of interest (RoI) is sent to the second

trigger level, the High Level Trigger (HLT).

The HLT receives readout data from the buffer, and then guided by the RoI applies additional

requirements to further reduce the event rate. The HLT can afford to be slower than the L1 trigger as

it has a small factor 400 times less events to consider. The HLT then makes the final decision whether

to accept or reject an event. The HLT reduces the 100kHz L1 event rate down to roughly 1. 2kHz

(3 kHz) for Run 2 (Run 3) that is stored and then analyzed offline. The trigger paths for Run 2 and

Run 3 are shown in figure 4.12.

The bandwidth of the HLT output is depicted in figure 4.13.

## 5

## Reconstruction

Converting detector readout into objects representing SM particles and signatures is a necessary inter-

mediate step in any ATLAS analysis. This step is referred to as reconstruction. As a hermetic multi-

purpose detector with a broad physics scope, ATLAS must be able to identify and infer properties of

as many SM particles as possible. The reconstruction algorithms used in this analysis were based on

release 22 (R22) of ATLAS software [51, 52]. This release is designed with Run 3 in mind, but is also

used for the Run 2 dataset in this analysis.

Most ATLAS analyses rely on a range of objects and reconstructed event properties. Having each

analysis develop tailored reconstruction algorithms for each relevant object type and event property

52


<!-- Page 72 -->


is prohibitively labor and CPU-hour intensive. As a result, dedicated combined performance (CP)

groups within ATLAS develop, maintain, update, and evaluate reconstruction algorithms. However,

due to the varying needs of physics analyses, the CP groups often provide a range of reconstruction

algorithms and recommended options that an analysis can choose from. The key reconstruction al-

gorithms and options used in this analysis are discussed in the following sections.

Reconstruction algorithm performance is generally evaluated with hybrid simulation and data-

driven methods. These studies are vital as they provide the systematic uncertainties that are used to

interpret the results of the analysis. Systematic uncertainties used in this analysis are discussed further

in chapter 8. Many of the systematic uncertainties are linked to a particular step or calibration of the

reconstruction algorithms described in this chapter.

There are roughly two layers to reconstruction. The first layer constructs basic constituents from

detector readout. There are three key basic constituents: ID tracks, topoclusters, and MS track seg-

ments. The ID tracks are used for all of the major reconstructed objects, and are discussed in section

5.1. Topoclusters are reconstructed from calorimeter readout and are used in various object recon-

struction algorithms as well. However, their most prominent role is in jet reconstruction. MS track

segments are used to reconstruct muons.

The precision of the ID tracks allows for the reconstruction of several vertices that seeded charged

particle tracks. The vertex reconstruction algorithm allows for the selection of a primary vertex, and

therefore the rejection of backgrounds from pileup vertices. Reconstructed vertices are also used for

various object and event-level variable reconstruction algorithms. Vertexing is discussed in section 5.2.

The basic constituents, ID tracks, topoclusters, and MS segments are used to reconstruct the final

analysis objects. These are generally: muons, electrons, hadronic taus, photons, and jets. However,

this analysis only considers muons, jets, and to a lesser extent electrons. Jet reconstruction, along with

topoclusterreconstruction, arediscussedinsection5.3. Jetsareacatch-allsignatureforQCD-charged

particles. Due to the excellent tracking capabilities of the ID, jets can be flavor-tagged. This analysis

53


<!-- Page 73 -->


relies on b-tagging, discussed in section 5.4. Muon reconstruction, along with MS track segment re-

construction, are discussed in section 5.5.

Besides object reconstruction, event-level properties are also reconstructed. The most useful event-

level property used in this analysis is missing transverse energy. Missing transverse energy is a rather

particular object, as it depends on the full spectrum of reconstructed objects in a given event to infer

momentum imbalance. Missing transverse energy is discussed in section 5.7.

5.1 Inner Tracking

ID tracks are a foundational intermediate component used for many higher-level reconstruction al-

gorithms. They serve as the primary input for identifying and measuring the kinematic properties of

charged particles (electrons, muons, and charged hadrons), as such they are also the key input to vertex

reconstruction.

5.1.1 Track Parameterization

Tracks at ATLAS represent the trajectory of charged particles through the detector. Since ATLAS

maintains a detailed magnetic field map throughout the ID (see section 4.2.1), a track’s trajectory

(roughly helical) is fully specified by a particle’s charge, and momentum at any given point along the

track. A standardized coordinate choice must be made for the parameterization of these trajectories.

The typical choice is to use as a reference point r0 the average position of proton-proton collisions1.

Let r be the track’s point of closest approach to the beamline. The track can then be described by the

following parameters:

• d0: the magnitude of the transverse component of r −r0. This is also the impact parameter.

5.1.2 Track Reconstruction

Naïvely there are two steps to reconstructing tracks: A) selecting hits from the inner detector read-

out and attributing them to a track candidate, and B) fitting the hits to retrieve the track parameters.

Practically, it proves useful to intertwine these steps, to have the selection of hits rely on intermediate

track candidate fits. The density of tracks for both Run 2 and Run 3 are so high, that a characteristic

track separation is roughly the size of the sensor channels – this makes track reconstruction a complex

task [40, 54, 55].

Clusterization. The first step to track reconstruction is the clusterization of raw measurements.

Each channel’s readout that passes a certain threshold is marked for clustering. These measurements

are then combined into clusters by simply grouping adjacent measurements. The readout from each

cluster is then used to create a space-point. It is worth noting that clusters will be further analyzed later

in the algorithm to determine whether clusters are consistent with signatures from single tracks or

multiple tracks passing near each other.

Track Candidates. The next step is to create track candidates. This step begins by creating track

seeds, sets of three space-points from consecutive inner pixel, and SCT layers in a straight line (the

tracks are not expected to bend much on the length-scale of a seed). These seeds are fit with a per-

fect helical trajectory. Various quality requirements are then applied to the set of seeds, including a

relatively small transverse impact parameter d0, as well as at the requirement of at least one more space-

point consistent with the helical trajectory in the layer above or below the seed. This step is necessary

to tame the CPU bandwidth for progressively more CPU intensive steps. The accepted seeds are then

extended along search roads by employing the Kalman filter (as described in section 5.1.3) to create

track candidates. This procedure involves iteratively adding space-points from consecutive layers to

the track candidate provided that the projected χ2 value of the track candidate is below a threshold.

Extending to TRT. These final inner tracks can then be extended to inside out tracks by consid-

points in the silicon detectors, the inner tracks are extended to inside out tracks by considering hits in

the TRT. However, if the addition of TRT hits makes the track fit worse, the silicon only inner tracks

are kept the way they are.

The inside out tracks have a high efficiency for reconstructing tracks originating from the primary

proton-proton collisions. However, outside in tracks are also useful in reconstructing tracks that may

have originated from a larger displacement from the interaction point. Outside in tracks use TRT

hits to create track candidates, and then extend the tracks back into the inner detector. Since the TRT

of interest for the track extensions.

5.1.3 Kalman Filter

This section describes the Kalman filter recursive fitting procedure and its use in the reconstruction

of tracks at ATLAS [56]. Kalman filters are a way of performing a recursive least squares fit of a set

of measurements, progressively adding new data points, and updating the fit. A common use case

for a Kalman filter is when measurements are made in real time, updating the state equation as more

data becomes available. In ATLAS, instead, Kalman filters are used offline. The reason why Kalman

filters are useful for tracking, is that they allow for a step-by-step selection of input space-points. In

58


<!-- Page 78 -->


particular, the iterative nature of the Kalman filter allows for a dedicated handling of outliers at each

step of the Kalman filter, while avoiding the computation cost of re-running a fit from scratch at each

step.

As an example consider inner tracking at ATLAS, which can be described roughly as:

1. An initial set of k noisy space-points yk from a track seed are fit with a helical path trajectory

xk (the subscript indicates this is the fit-result of the k space-points).

2. A new space-point yk+1 from an adjacent layer is considered. Its consistency with the model

xk is evaluated (as a χ2 k+1,k value).

3. The result is used to determine how to update the model xk to xk+1. A threshold on the

χ2 k+1,k value is imposed. If χ2 k+1,k is too high, the new space-point is considered an outlier,

andthealgorithmproceedstothenextlayerxk+1 = xk. Ifthevalueisbelowthethreshold, the

model is updated to xk+1 via the Kalman filter. The algorithm returns to step 2, proceeding

recursively.

Practically there are often multiple space-points yk+1 from adjacent layers that are within the χ2 k+1,k

threshold. In this case, the tracking algorithm will diverge, creating a track candidate for each such

space-point. Track ambiguities are resolved later.

5.3 Jets

Jets at ATLAS are reconstructed analysis objects, with four-momenta, designed to reproduce the kine-

matic properties of a high-energy QCD parton. The signature this analysis targets includes a high en-

ergy muon and a b-quark. Since the quark is charged under QCD, jet-reconstruction is indispensable

in producing the targeted final state. Jet reconstruction is also necessary to reconstruct the event’s

missing transverse energy, which is another key variable in this analysis.

5.3.1 Showering and Hadronization

Tomotivatethejet reconstructionmethodsusedbyATLAS,asketchofjetformationisuseful. Events

deemed interesting by most ATLAS analyses feature energy exchanges well above the soft QCD scale

ΛQCD ∼100 MeV. In this limit, the underlying hard-scattering event, and low-energy QCD inter-

actions factorize. As a result matrix element calculations can be performed for any given SM or BSM

process, before and separately from considering the soft-QCD phenomenology to follow. As such,

the output of a hard-scattering calculation is the first step in the jet-formation process.

The output of a hard-scattering calculation, on paper, is a differential cross-section. Practically

speaking, these differential cross-sections are instead represented as a high-statistics sample of MC

events. These events can be considered a sampling of the analytic differential cross-section. Each event

is effectively just a list of fundamental particles and their properties [61]. This list of particles could

containstable, or semi-stable particles like leptons and photons. However, it couldalso contain QCD-

charged particles like quarks and gluons. This list of particles is sometimes referred to as the parton-

level event.

Any given hard-scattering calculation seeding the parton-level event, was truncated at a given order.

64


<!-- Page 84 -->


In principle, the contribution from an additional gluon radiation could always be included, however

includingthisradiationatthematrix-elementcalculationlevelwouldinvolvegoingtoonehigherorder

in perturbation theory to cancel the newly introduced IR-divergence. Such an approach makes matrix

element calculations intractable after just a few radiations. Instead of tackling additional emissions at

the matrix-element level, final-state QCD partons are showered.

The showering process is set up as an evolution, where quarks and gluons evolve, emitting more

quarks and gluons according to the QCD splitting functions. A common evolution parameter used

for showering is the showered particle’s energy scale. This parameter decreases as the shower evolves,

and the available energy is shared by an increasing number of partons. The evolution is truncated once

parton energies approach the energy scale where this perturbative picture breaks down, and color-

confinement kicks in. It is worth noting that the set of showered partons pick up some transverse

momentum upon splitting, but are preferentially emitted collinear to the parton seeding the splitting.

As such, each high-energy QCD particle from the parton-level event tends to seed a set of showered

lower-energy QCD particles with momenta within a characteristic solid-angle centered on the initial

parton’s momentum.

Although the showering description above stemmed from a final-state parton, and therefore de-

scribed a final-state shower, a coherent picture also necessitates initial state showering. The initial

state showering differs in that it mandates backward evolution, to higher particle energies.

The forward shower stops near the ΛQCD scale where perturbative QCD methods fail. At this

point a list of QCD particles quarks, and gluons, have to be mapped onto the hadronic particles that

are observed. This mapping, called hadronization, is not well understood. Several numeric methods

guided by QCD principles exist for hadronization. The two most common methods used in high en-

ergyphysicsarethestring model, andcluster model[62]. Threeeventgenerationsoftwarepackagesare

usedforshoweringandhadronizationinthisanalysis. Herwig[63]andSherpa[64]employthecluster

model of hadronization, while Pythia [65] employs the string model. The output of the hadroniza-

65


<!-- Page 85 -->


tion step is a list of hadrons and their kinematic properties. The combination of these hadrons with

any stable particles4 from the parton-level event, can be seen as the final theoretical prediction, and

is often referred to as the particle-level event. Recall that each high energy particle from the parton-

level event seeded a cone of showered partons centered around the high-energy particle’s momentum.

Post-hadronization, these QCD-charged particles are converted to color-confined hadrons within the

collimated cone. By momentum conservation, the sum of their momenta matches the parton-level

particle’s momentum. This set of hadrons constitute a jet, and as such a jet is the expected signature

of a high-energy parton-level QCD charged particle.

5.3.2 Anti-kT

A jet-reconstruction algorithm, conceptually, undoes the hadronization and shower. Jet reconstruc-

tion algorithms cluster together particles, tracks, or other objects with four-momenta, and then sum

the four-momenta to retrieve the jet’s kinematic properties. Various definitions for jets existed in the

past, however, by the LHC-era standardized approaches to clustering jets have been adopted [66–68].

High energy collider experiments in particular use the anti-kT algorithm.

The algorithm takes as an input a list of four-momenta, and as such, this algorithm is just as well

defined for truth-level particles, as it is for energy deposits and tracks observed in detectors. The inputs

to the algorithm used by ATLAS are discussed in subsections 5.3.3 and 5.3.4.

The Anti-kT algorithm is a member of the sequential recombination jet algorithm family. A key

property of this family of clustering algorithms is that it does not impose a rigid cone-shape on jets.

The algorithm features just one tunable parameter, the R parameter, which is an indicator for the

angular size of the target jets. The algorithm takes as an input a list of four-vectors S. The two metrics

The particle-flow (PFlow) algorithm takes as an input a selection of ID tracks, and the full list of an

5.4 Flavor Tagging

Jets reconstructed by ATLAS can be seeded by a variety of different particles. Although some particles

yield indistinguishable signatures (like all light quarks), others have particular properties that can be

exploited to tag a jet with a specific flavor. The prime example and primary benchmark for flavor-

tagging is the b-quark – which is also a key flavor tag in this analysis.

Consider again the QCD showering and hadronization process, as described in section 5.3.1, with

the added detail that the particle that seeded the QCD shower was a heavy flavor quark, like a b-quark

(or c-quark). Since QCD alone cannot violate flavor number(s), the particle content after the QCD

shower is bound to include a quark of the same flavor as the initial heavy flavor quark. Hadronization,

74


<!-- Page 94 -->


as a QCD process, also must preserve flavor, and as such a corresponding heavy flavor baryon will be

produced by the hadronization process. Heavy flavor baryons are special – they are long-lived com-

pared to QCD, but decay through weak force mediated processes in ∼1.5 ps. A relativistic b-flavored

hadron will therefore have a mean flight length from a few millimeters to a few centimeters before

decaying. This displaced decay is simulated in MC samples as the final layer after the hadronization

process. For most samples used in this analysis, the package EvtGen [76] was used to simulate the

displaced decays. Note EvtGen handles not only b-hadron decays, but also c-hadron and tau lepton

decays.

The excellent tracking capabilities of the ID allow for track reconstruction to expose the displaced

vertices of these unstable particles. Individual tracks will feature larger than expected impact param-

eters to the primary vertex. For decays that featured multiple charged decay products, the collection

of tracks could also triangulate a displaced vertex. For Run 1 analyses, b-tagging algorithms were de-

signed manually, using the physics intuition of displaced decays. However, flavor-tagging has evolved

considerably since then by employing various machine learning algorithms. A combination of man-

ual algorithms, boosted decision trees, and neural networks based on intermediate variables were used

to great avail during Run 2 [77]. However, the most recent and effective flavor-tagging algorithm

used by ATLAS, GN2 [78], was trained directly on input jet and track properties. GN2 is used for

b-tagging in this analysis.

GN2 uses as an input a jet, and up to 40 tracks that are associated with the jet by angular distance.

Note, the tracks need not necessarily have been used in the particle-flow algorithm in the jet’s recon-

struction. Each jet contributes just two features, pT and η, whereas each track contributes a range of

features that not only include the kinematic properties of the track, but also uncertainties on those

properties, as well as track-reconstruction level information like number of hits on specific tracking

detector sub-systems and even whether those hits featured any special properties (e.g. whether pixel

hits were considered “shared”). See [79] for a full list of input features (note however that “holes” have

5.5 Muons

Tracks that make it past the calorimeter system are quite reliably assumed to be left by muons. As

such tracks, and track segments in the MS can be used to tag ID tracks as muons, and improve mo-

mentum measurements thanks to the toroidal magnetic fields around the MS. Muon reconstruction

relies on first reconstructing MS track segments and MS track candidates from the MS detector sub-

system. ThesemeasurementsarethencombinedwithIDtracks, andevencalorimeterenergydeposits,

to reconstruct muon objects [80].

5.5.1 MS Tracks and Segments

The first step in MS tracking is MS track segment reconstruction. Track segments are reconstructed

within each MS station, by assuming straight-line trajectories to start with. This is a reasonable as-

sumption provided the limited bending of a muon track within a MS station. Segments from dif-

ferent MS stations are then combined into preliminary MS tracks by a loose requirement following a

first order approximation for the track’s trajectory. Recall the MS stations resolve only the one pre-

cision coordinate of tracks (z in the barrel, R in the endcap). At this point the other coordinate ϕ is

appended from the muon trigger system detectors.

These track candidates, that are at this point essentially collections of hits, are then fitted by a global

77


<!-- Page 97 -->


χ2 fit, taking into account the true magnetic field map. Track parameters are generally the same as

they were in section 5.1 (i.e. track parameters near the interaction point). The fitting procedure,

that involves multiple fits can remove outliers, pickup additional hits, and account for energy loss in

calorimeters and detector material. Both final MS tracks, as well as their track segment building blocks

are used for muon reconstruction, by combining them with ID tracks. Finally, just like for the inner

tracking algorithm, an ambiguity resolver decides whether to reject or keep partially overlapping MS

tracks.

5.5.2 Muon Types and Working Points

Muons at ATLAS are reconstructed using a handful of different algorithms. These different algo-

rithms stitch together ID tracks, MS tracks, MS track segments, as well as hits throughout the ID,

MS, and even calorimeters in different ways. Generally there are five ATLAS muon types, where each

type reflects a different muon reconstruction algorithm. Beyond the muon types there are also sug-

gested working points (WPs) for muons. Each working point places a set of requirements on accepted

muons, these requirements can include the muon type. This analysis uses High-pT working point

muons. This working point accepts only two types of muons:

• Combined (CB) muons: to reconstruct a CB muon, a MS track is extrapolated back to the

ID, and found to match an ID track. A new fit is then performed over the hits from both

tracks. This fit includes energy loss in the calorimeters. This process can also update the input

hits of the track. This is the simplest muon type, where the muon’s track was independently

reconstructed in both the ID and MS.

• Inside-Out (IO) muons: The IO muons rely on a reconstructed ID track, but loosen the re-

quirement of a matching MS track. Instead, ID tracks are extrapolated to the MS, and if three

loosely matching MS hits are found, a fit is performed over the ID track hits and MS hits as

78


<!-- Page 98 -->


well as calorimeter energy loss. Including IO muons recover muons that for some reason were

not reconstructed in the MS. They are conceptually looser, and therefore increase muon re-

construction efficiency.

A further description of ATLAS muon types, as well as descriptions of the other three muon types

(not used in this analysis) are presented in [80].

Multiple WPs are defined to suit the different needs of physics analyses. When selecting muons

there is an inevitable trade-off between reconstruction efficiency and purity. A tighter WP will result

in a high purity but lower efficiency. A looser WP will boost efficiency at the cost of contamination.

There are three primary muon WPs at ATLAS: Tight, Medium, and Loose. The specialized High-pT

WP used in this analysis is built on top of the Medium WP.

Within the ID acceptance |η| < 2.5, which is also the muon region of interest for this analysis,

there are three selection criteria for Medium WP muons: A) muons must be CB or IO, B) muons

must feature at least two MS precision stations, C) there is a requirement on ID-to-MS q/p com-

patibility. A muon is considered to feature a MS precision station if the muon features at least three

hits from that station. Recall, for most solid-angles muons would pass through three MS precision

stations5. The ratio of a particle’s charge over momentum, q/p, is a natural intermediary variable in

track reconstruction, stemming from track curvature. This variable is evaluated separately for the ID

and MS components of each Medium WP muon candidate. A compatibility metric is then defined as

the magnitude of the difference between the ID and MS q/p values, divided by the sum in quadrature

of the errors on each of these q/p variables. As such this ratio is in essence a significance-based com-

patibility metric. For Medium WP muons this quantity must be less than 7. Medium WP muons

have other requirements for |η| > 2.5, however such muons do not pass the selection of muons in

this analysis.

The High-pT working point is tailored for selecting high momentum muons that retain high qual-

ity, and thereby introduce less error. A dedicated WP for high momentum muons is useful because

high momentum muons exhibit minimal bending, and therefore their momentum measurement is

less precise. To avoid muon reconstruction errors from knee-capping the analysis’ sensitivity, muon

selection criteria can be tightened to only accept high momentum muons that exhibit other proper-

ties indicative of a reliable momentum measurement. The specific requirements placed on High-pT

WP muons are quite case-based, and are summarized in [80]. In general, tighter MS precision station

requirements are applied. These requirements ensure that candidate muons feature measurements

across a longer path in the MS, and therefore should see more B-field induced bending. Furthermore,

there are also tailored selections in regions where relative detector alignments are less reliable. An ad-

ditional requirement is placed on the overall track’s post-fit q/p uncertainty. The requirement is not

a simple threshold and depends on detector geometry as well as the muon’s pT. Figure 5.9 shows

the q/p resolution for muons evaluated in MC simulations for Run 2 conditions. The resolution is

derived by fitting a Gaussian to |(q/p)Reco −(q/p)Truth|/(q/p)Truth.

5.6 Other ATLAS Objects

Besides muons and jets, ATLAS also has standardized electron, photon, and hadronic tau lepton re-

construction. These reconstruction algorithms are not discussed further here as they have a limited

(or no) effect on the presented analysis. The analysis does define baseline electrons as objects, however

the only purpose they serve is to veto events with any electrons. Naturally the event selection does as

a result depend on the electron definition, however it is not too sensitive to the particularities of the

reconstruction and so are not discussed further here.

Hadronic tau leptons and photons can also be reconstructed by ATLAS. However this analysis is

entirely inclusive to these objects, and for all intents and purposes does not reconstruct them. The

footprints of “truth” taus and photons is still effectively included in the missing transverse energy

reconstruction through their constituents, as discussed in the following section.

5.7 Missing Transverse Energy

Transverse missing energy Emiss T is a powerful variable for many ATLAS analysis [81], including the

analysis presented in this thesis. Since neutrinos are nominally the only SM particle type that pass

through ATLAS without interacting, Emiss T serves as a smoking gun for physics processes featuring

neutrinos. In this analysis cuts on the Emiss T significance S(Emiss T ) are especially powerful in sup-

pressing background processes, and as such S(Emiss T ) and by extension Emiss T is a key variable to this

analysis.

Missing transverse energy, is often considered a two-component vector Emiss T since the transverse

direction of momentum-imbalance has two components. Indeed, it would be more accurate to refer

to Emiss T as missing transverse momentum, however missing transverse energy and missing transverse

The principle of reconstructing Emiss T is especially simple: find the momentum imbalance of all

6.1 Dataset

This analysis employs the full ATLAS Run 2 dataset that was recorded from 2015 to 2018 as well as

the partial Run 3 dataset from 2022 and 2023. The Run 2 dataset amounts to an integrated lumi-

nosity of 140 fb−1 whereas Run 3 amounts to 55fb−1. These datasets must be studied in parallel

due to several major differences between the runs. For starters, the Run 2 dataset collides protons at

a center of mass energy of √s = 13 TeV whereas the Run 3 dataset is at √s = 13.6 TeV. As a result

the underlying invariant mass spectrum for each run is different. Furthermore, the ATLAS detector

itself was upgraded, and therefore data-taking conditions, as well as data-acquisition changed. Many

reconstruction algorithms were also updated. So for all intents and purposes, a separate measurement

is made on the Run 2 and Run 3 datasets. The only combined interpretation in this analysis is at the

model-dependent hypothesis test level (presented in section 10.3).

The first step in selecting a dataset, is the choice of a trigger. The trigger can be seen as the first live

cut applied. For this analysis the lowest unprescaled muon triggers were used. Prescaling for triggers

is the practice of only storing a fraction of the events that actually passed a trigger requirement, and

effectively up-scaling their contribution to what would have been the full trigger rate. To avoid com-

plexities, this analysis does not use such prescaled triggers, and instead uses the most inclusive muon

triggers that do not apply any prescaling. The list of the triggers used for various data taking periods

are listed in table 6.1. Generally there are two types of triggers that are accepted for each period, one

with an isolation requirement, and one without. The muon trigger that does not include isolation

targets muons with pT > 50 GeV for all data taking periods. The muon trigger that does include

isolation requirements reduce the trigger rate, and thereby permit lower pT trigger thresholds. The

isolatedmuontriggershaveapT thresholdbetween20−26 GeVdependingonthedatatakingperiod.

The specific isolation requirements for those triggers also vary by data taking period. More details on

It is worth noting that this analysis was performed in parallel with other lepton plus jet flavor chan-

6.3.1 Muons

This analysis targets a TeV scale resonant muon plus b-jet. The muon is likely to carry a significant

fraction of the available momentum, and as such is expected to be high-energy. For this reason the

HighPt muon reconstruction working point is used that prioritizes high-energy muons. Muon re-

construction as well as the selection requirements of muons for this working point was discussed in

section 5.5.

The analysis identifies and uses two types of muons, the more inclusive muons are referred to as

are considered for missing transverse energy reconstruction (section 5.7), and B) they are used in the

Reconstructed and selected objects can overlap in different ways. For one, objects can overlap in solid

6.5 Preselection

After committing to a trigger choice, and identifying the datasets to be studied, the first layer of cuts

filtering events offline is the preselection. The preselection serves to clean data, remove trigger effects,

and narrow the focus of the analysis to an event-space where the chosen MC yields are in rough agree-

ment with data yields.

First an event-cleaning based on ATLAS recommendations is performed. This includes removing

incomplete events, as well as events for which a specific detector subsystem indicated corrupted data.

Also according to ATLAS recommendations, any event that features a jet that does not pass the loose

jet cleaning criteria is rejected [96].

Next, events are filtered by their object content. In particular, events are required to have either

one or two signal muons, and no additional electrons. The events must also not have any additional

jet are each required to have at least pT > 130 GeV. The invariant mass of the leading jet and leading

muon mℓj must be larger than 700 GeV. Further, for events that feature two muons, the invariant

resonances are likely to give not only the one high energy lepton from the heavy resonance, but also

an additional softer lepton. For this reason this analysis targets the muon plus b-jet invariant mass

spectrum in two signal regions: the single-lepton (SR-1L) region, and the two-lepton (SR-2L) region.

The benchmark signal model ˜S1 is used to motivate signal region selections. However, a discussion

97


<!-- Page 117 -->


Adhering to the norm in collider physics, this analysis specifies the invariant mass spectrum within

each signal region as a binned template (i.e. histogram). The factors motivating the range and binning

of this template include available expected event statistics, as well as the detector resolution on the

variable of interest: mℓj. This is discussed in further detail in section 7.1.

As alluded to in section 6.2, SM processes that feature electroweak interactions are generally rea-

sonably well modeled by generated MC datasets. For this reason, there is a long-standing precedent in

high energy physics to use a MC dataset to model the shape of a distribution for a particular process.

The shape refers not only to the relative yields of bins within a signal region, but across all regions

being considered in the analysis. The normalization for a particular process’ template is in contrast

derived in a data-driven way. In particular, a maximum likelihood fit is performed that includes a

free-floating overall normalization factor for the template of each major background process. The fit

is performed not only on the signal regions, but also includes control regions (CRs). There is at least

one dedicated single-bin control region for each major background process. The control regions are

by design depleted of signal events, but saturated in events from a specific background process. As a

result, the normalization of the background templates throughout signal regions and control regions

will in large part be set by event yields in the dedicated control regions. The likelihood used in this fit

is described in section 7.2.

The MC templates entering the maximum likelihood fit are not entirely rigid. Systematic uncer-

tainties, derived separately, are included as auxiliary terms in the fit. Unlike the normalization factors

of the templates which are free-floating, these auxiliary terms incur loss if the systematic uncertain-

ties’ respective nuisance parameter is pulled away from its nominal value. Systematic uncertainties are

discussed in chapter 8.

A discussion on this analysis’ major backgrounds, as well as studies motivating the selection for

SR-1L and SR-2L are presented in section 7.3. This analysis’ background modeling strategy as well as

the method for validating that strategy is described in section 7.4.

7.1 mℓj Binning

The targeted resonant muon plus b-jet signatures would be localized around a certain (unknown)

value of mℓj. For this reason, an analysis strategy including a binned signal region in mℓj is motivated.

Although there is no widespread general method for optimizing a binning prescription, this analysis

considers two guiding principles. First, bin widths are set such that bin widths are larger than the

resolution of the mℓj variable. Second, all bins must retain sufficient expected event yields to retain

statistical power, and ensure MC-modeling remains reliable.

Choosing bin widths to be larger than mℓj resolution limits the migration of events between bins.

In other words if the particle-level (“truth”) event has a certain mℓj, then a bin centered at that mℓj

value with a width of 2σmℓj would have a 68% chance of registering in that bin. Naturally, migration

effects due to experimentaleffectsare generallyratherwellmodeled, andreasonabledata-to-MCagree-

ment is also seen for finer binning. However, a wider binning serves as an insurance policy against mis-

modeling of the experimental migration effects. The resolution-based binning also ensures that the

majority of resonant events should enter one or two bins, thereby not diluting the signal’s statistical

power for already low expected event yields.

Several studies in MC were performed to determine the mℓj resolution. Since relative muon reso-

lution σpT/pT scales linearly with pT, the invariant mass resolution is also expected to deteriorate

trapolations.

the VRs must have sufficient statistics to overcome Poisson errors for validation.

7.4.4 Signal Contamination

The validation strategy relies on matching background estimates to data in the validation regions.

However, these testsshould nothavethe powerto exposeanysignalhypothesis. Assuchthevalidation

regionsmustnothaveastatisticallysignificantfraction(i.e. contamination)ofsignalevents. Naturally,

since the major background normalization factors are set by the control region yields, the CRs should

also be free of any signal contamination.

There is, however, an unavoidable trade-off. Generally, it is favorable to have both CRs and VRs

as close to the SRs as possible to simplify extrapolations. On the other hand the signal templates are

distributed continuously, and as such, the validation regions can only be so close to the signal regions

before they pick up too many signal events. Therefore some validation regions are in fact expected to

have a non-zero signal contamination.

In principle, the maximum amount of acceptable signal contamination could be evaluated by sen-

sitivity studies. However, this is overkill for the purposes of this analysis. Instead, 10% is seen as a

reasonable upper limit, especially for regions/bins with low statistics where Poisson errors alone could

account for 10% fluctuations.

Signal contamination is evaluated as a percentage for all 24 generated signal points for all control

and validation regions. Since the signal grid starts at signal points that have long-since been excluded,

and ends at signal points well outside of this analysis’ reach, the contamination percentages are also

expected to span a wide range. Note, as mentioned in section 2.4, prior studies have already excluded

LQs that couple b quarks and muons up to 1.7 TeV [20]. For this reason, signal contamination in

excess of 10% for signal points below this threshold are considered acceptable.

## 8

## Uncertainties

The nominal background and signal hypotheses in this analysis are simply event yields per region per

bin, i.e.: templates. Different uncertainties are therefore naturally represented as variations of these

templates. As such there are two (not necessarily symmetric) templates for each uncertainty corre-

sponding to the ±1σ variations from that uncertainty.

These templates, were already mentioned when discussing the likelihood in section 7.2. Specifi-

cally, ν0 rbs was the s sample’s, r region’s, b bin’s nominal value, and ν± rbs,κ were the ±1σ variations

on that template for the κ systematic uncertainty. Each of these template-based uncertainties were

assigned a single nuisance parameter ακ and included in the likelihood (equation 7.4) for the purpose

127


<!-- Page 147 -->


of performing fits, deriving post-fit uncertainties, and combining uncertainties. These ακ account for

the vast majority of nuisance parameters in the fit, and therefore also for the vast majority of system-

atics (both experimental and theoretical). The experimental template-based systematics are discussed

further in section 8.1, and the theoretical template-based systematics are discussed further in section

8.2.

Besides the template-based uncertainties, there is also a single luminosity nuisance parameter λ (in

units of fb−1) representing the total integrated luminosity uncertainty. It is based on a luminosity

measurement λ0 with a symmetric uncertainty: σλ [101–103]. Purely per-bin, MC-statistics based

uncertainties are also considered, even though they are generally small. Both of these uncertainties are

included as perfectly Gaussian, but could be seen as templates symmetrically straddling the nominal

prediction.

The final source of uncertainty comes from the free-floating normalization factors µs that are used

in the fit to scale specific process overall yields. By and large, high statistic control regions that are satu-

rated in events of a particular process constrain these parameters. These are effectively methodological

uncertainties, and they are derived only after fitting by scanning the conditional maximum likelihood

for each normalization factor one by one.

For the template-based uncertainties, the categorization of theoretical and experimental uncertain-

ties can in part be understood by tracing the steps in the overall MC simulation. Theoretical un-

certainties should include all uncertainties up to the particle-level event, i.e. a list of color-confined

stable particles and their momenta. Experimental uncertainties should account for all uncertainties

from this point forth, i.e. all the detector and reconstruction effects. The uncertainties from the

free-floating normalization factors are methodological uncertainties that effectively capture both the-

oretical and experimental effects relating to the scaling of overall yields of background processes in a

data-driven way.

8.1 Experimental Uncertainties

Most of the uncertainties in this analysis are experimental. Dedicated working groups in ATLAS that

studied the effects of different reconstruction algorithms and detector properties made recommenda-

tions for how to include experimental uncertainties for various effects.

Many of these uncertainties are designed to be evaluated in a weight-based manner. For instance,

consider a dedicated measurement of the reconstruction efficiency for a particular object. For a given

MC event, the per-object efficiency has to be compounded for each such reconstructed object to de-

rive an effective event-efficiency. This efficiency then scales MC event weights to account for the ex-

perimental reconstruction efficiency effect. Similarly, up and down variations from the two-sided

efficiency measurement can be used to assign up and down variation weights to the same MC event.

To derive the up and down variation templates, the MC events simply need to be histogrammed for

each weight variation.

Instead of using event-wide weights, some uncertainties are derived with a tree-based approach. In

this case, up and down variations of systematic uncertainties simply modify object properties, and

thereby, events can migrate in and out of the analysis’ acceptance. Naturally, this will have an effect

on the templates derived by histogramming the MC events even if weights do not change.

The experimental uncertainties are assigned to reconstructed object properties and reconstructed

event-variable properties. The relevant reconstruction algorithms used for this analysis were summa-

rized in chapter 5. Many of the systematic uncertainties correspond to specific steps, procedures, and

calibrations in the reconstruction chain, however, the auxiliary measurements used to derive these sys-

tematics are not detailed here. Instead, a high-level specification by object/property type is presented

below.

Since this analysis uses muon triggers, and uses either one or two signal muons for each analysis

event, muon uncertainties are important. Table 8.1 shows the experimental uncertainties on muons

## Validation

Before unblinding, and fitting directly to the data in signal regions, control-region only fits were per-

formed, and the results studied to evaluate whether the proposed background modeling strategy was

sound. It was – and this chapter details why.

First, the background hypothesis is fit to the control regions only via an MLE fit. The likelihood

for this fit is described in section 7.2. The signal normalization µLQ is set to zero, and only four data

points nrb are fit for each run, representing the observed yields of the four control regions. The fits for

Run2andRun3decoupleastherearenocorrelatedparametersbetweenthetworuns. Thefirstsanity

check comes from the fit results themselves described in section 9.1. Next, the best-fit parameters can

139


<!-- Page 159 -->


be used to construct important kinematic distributions in the control regions. These distributions

are presented in section 9.2. The distributions give an indication of whether extrapolations into SRs

promise to be well-modeled.

Next, the fit parameters from the control region only fits are extrapolated into validation regions.

Since the validation regions are orthogonal to the control regions, the overall normalizations of pre-

dicted yields are no longer guaranteed to match observed yields. Comparing the extrapolated vali-

dation region yields to the observed yields with an expectation of reasonable closure, is the topic of

section 9.3. This constitutes the primary benchmark for validation. Kinematic distributions for these

regions are also presented in section 9.4. Overall good agreement is observed in the validation regions,

and the validation is considered successful.

It is worth re-iterating that the final set of fit parameters from the control region only fits do not

constitutethefinalbackgroundhypothesis. Theyjustservetovalidatethebackgroundmodelingstrat-

egy. The final background only hypothesis employs the same strategy, but also includes signal regions

into the fit. This is the topic of the next chapter.

9.2 Kinematic Distributions in CRs

Prior to checking the fit results extrapolated to other, adjacent regions, it makes sense to check the

fit results within the fitted control regions. In particular, it is worthwhile checking the kinematic

distributions of the key variables used in the analysis.

Post-fit distributions are derived by creating the full set of MC templates for each variable in ques-

tion, and then applying the final set of fit parameters to modify the templates. Essentially, the yield-

model described in section 7.2 still holds for variables within the control regions, even though the

binned distributions are not fitted. Constructing the kinematic distributions involves deriving nomi-

nal MC templates for any given channel r, bin b, and sample s: ν0 rbs, as well as the full set of systematic

uncertainty templates κ for that bin and sample: ν± rbs,κ. With these templates, the equation 7.6 can

be evaluated at the best-fit parameters ˆµ and ˆθ from the control region only fit to give the post-fit

distribution. This requires evaluating the full set of templates for each channel in each region. This is

done exactly for all experimental systematic uncertainties. However, the theoretical uncertainties for

the post-fit distributions are derived just once, inclusively, for each region. The inclusive theoretical

uncertainty is then used for each bin of each kinematic distribution within the region.

Kinematic distributions for all variables used in the selection were constructed and studied. How-

ever, the distributions that are particularly interesting are the ones that feature a cut that was inverted,

or changed, for a particular control region with respect to signal regions. By this logic the most inter-

esting distributions per control region are:

• WCR: S(Emiss T ) since this cut was inverted. pT/mℓj since this cut was loosened.

• ZCR: mℓℓsince this cut was inverted.

• TCR-high-mℓj and TCR-low-mℓj: Nb since this cut was inverted. S(Emiss T ) since signal,

validation, and control regions were sliced in this variable.

The distributions for the other variables are shown in the appendix D.1.

*Figure 9.3 shows the post-fit distributions for the S(Emiss T ) and pT/mℓj variables in the W+jets*

control regions. Generally a reasonable agreement between data and MC is observed. Most notably,

S(Emiss T ) does not seem to have any discernible slope projecting downward, the direction in which

extrapolations to VRs and SRs are made. Similarly there is no discernible slope in pT/mℓj around the

0.3 threshold. Recall the SR-1Ls feature a pT/mℓj > 0.3 cut while the W control regions feature a

pT/mℓj > 0.2cut. Thereisarguablyaveryslightshapein∆R(l, j)(appendixfigureD.1). However,

the fluctuations are largely within uncertainties, and furthermore, recall that the ∆R(l, j) cut was

loose to the point of being almost inclusive, and as such features in this variable would have less of an

impact.

The Z+jets control regions feature fewer statistics than the W+jets regions, since two lepton events

are rarer than single lepton events. This is especially true away from the Z peak. The most relevant cut

for this region was on mℓℓ. Figure 9.4 shows the post-fit distributions for mℓℓfor each run. Again, the

agreement is reasonable despite higher fluctuations from lower statistics. The mℓℓdistribution does

not feature a discernible slope on either end. However, the extrapolation is hard to have a rigorous

9.3 Extrapolation into VRs

The real test of whether the chosen analysis strategy is sound relies on checking if fit results extrapolate

well into adjacent regions. These adjacent regions, the validation regions, were chosen to straddle

signal regions as closely as possible. Their definitions are summarized in section 7.4. The majority of

validation regions sit at high mℓj, and preserve the same binning as the signal regions, for as long as

statistics allow.

The extrapolation into these regions is performed by deriving the full set of templates across all bins

for all regions, just like for the kinematic distributions in the control regions described in section 9.2.

The only difference is that these extrapolations also evaluate theoretical uncertainties by bin (recall

they were evaluated inclusively for the kinematic distributions).

*Figure 9.7 shows the yield distributions in the validation regions. The figure also includes a sub-*

panel that evaluates the agreement between data and MC as a significance. This significance estimate

is calculated by using the significance estimate akin to equation 7.8, only including systematic er-

rors; the functional form can be found in [100]. Overall there are two low-mℓj validation regions

(VR-S(Emiss T ) and TVR-low-mℓj), and nine high mℓj validation regions. Overall, good agreement

is observed between data and the post-fit templates. The Run 2 regions show no tension above 1σ.

The Run 3 regions show no tension above 2σ. There is also no clearly discernible shape mismodeling.

The slightly higher tensions for Run 3 can be in part be attributed to the lower statistics, and how

the significance is evaluated. In particular, the method for evaluating the significance relies on a large

event-number approximation. Although this approximation has been shown to work reasonably well

for smaller event counts, it gives slight over-estimates for lower statistics. Overall, the observed yields

are close enough to the control region only fit expected yields for the validation to be considered suc-

cessful.

9.4 Kinematic distributions in VRs

Just like the kinematic distributions in the control regions were studied, so too can the kinematic

distributions in the validation regions be studied. Note that for the kinematic distributions, just like

before, the experimental uncertainties are derived bin by bin, whereas theoretical uncertainties are

derived inclusively in the particular region. Although all the key variables were modeled in all of the

validation regions, the most important kinematic variables per region are the ones whose cuts differ

from the signal regions. These variables per region are:

## Results

The unblinded results of this analysis can be scrutinized through two lenses. First, the agreement be-

tween the background only hypothesis and data is examined. Tensions are found to be small, with no

smoking gun pointing at new physics. For anyone who considers the muon plus b-jet resonant phase

space to be a motivated region for BSM physics, this unblinded mℓj spectrum with an overlayed back-

ground SM model is in itself a model-independent result. Second, hypothesis tests are performed for

benchmark LQ signals. The prior ATLAS pair production limits on LQs [20] (mLQ > 1710 GeV)

couplingtomuonsandb-quarksareimprovedforcouplingsstartingaroundyµb ∼1.0. Thesemodel-

specific results are useful for establishing a metric for the sensitivity of this analysis.

10.1 CR+SR Fits

The first step in evaluating the background hypothesis’ agreement to data is to construct the back-

ground hypothesis itself. This is done by performing a maximum likelihood fit over control regions

and signal regions. Again, the likelihood function from section 7.2 is used with µLQ = 0. The mea-

surements, i.e. data points, being fit to (nrb) span the four single bin control regions as well as the

four plus three signal region bins for each run. This amounts to 11 data points for each run. Since the

fit parameters are not correlated, and the datasets are orthogonal, the fits decouple, and are therefore

performed and studied separately for each run. The background hypothesis can then be constructed

from MC templates (ν0 rbs, νrbs,κ±) and the best fit values of the parameters (ˆµ, ˆθ) via equation 7.6.

The fit results are expected to resemble the results from the control region only fit, however, they

are not expected to be identical due to the additional data points from the signal regions. The nor-

malization factors derived in this fit are presented in table 10.1. They retain the overall trends that

the control region only fit normalization factors did – namely, the V +jets backgrounds are scaled up,

whereas the top backgrounds are scaled down. The top normalization factors also retain similar prop-

erties. Namely, that there is a sizable separation between the high-mℓj and low-mℓj top normalization

factors in Run 2, whereas in Run 3, the difference is much smaller.

Since the number of data points entering the fits (11) is larger than the number of free floating pa-

rameters (4), the fit is over-constrained, and data is not expected to match the prediction perfectly. For

157


<!-- Page 177 -->


this reason, the nuisance parameters from the auxiliary terms will be pulled away from their nominal

values, contributing some loss as they do. Figure 10.1 shows the pulls on the nuisance parameters. It

is reassuring to see that all of the fitted nuisance parameters are well within the 1-sigma error bars, and

that in fact only a small subset of them are pulled away from their nominal values. The parameters

that are pulled the most for Run 2 relate to the jet energy resolution uncertainties. There are two

parameters that feature noticeable pulls for Run 3: the non-closure uncertainty on jet energy scale, as

well as the muon reconstruction efficiency uncertainty. The muon reconstruction uncertainties for

Run 3 were known to be large, at the time of this analysis, as the final set of studies calibrating muons

and setting tighter recommended uncertainties was not yet complete.

As expected, the pulls on nuisance parameters give rise to correlations between nuisance param-

eters. Figure 10.2 shows the correlation matrices for the two runs for the control plus signal region

fit. Nuisance parameter co-correlations are all quite small. For Run 2, two flavor tagging uncertainties

seem to have a small anti-correlation. For Run 3, again, the jet non closure uncertainty on energy scale

as well as the muon reconstruction efficiency have correlations with a range of nuisance parameters.

The correlations to normalization factors are naturally larger. Overall the correlations resemble the

ones seen in the control region only fit. Each template’s normalization factor is correlated with theo-

retical uncertainties on that template, and the top normalization factors have strong co-correlations.

The control plus signal region fit results conform to rough expectations, and there are no red flags

in the mechanics of the fit.

Equation 10.2, also sometimes referred to as CLs+b, can be interpreted as the probability of hav-

ing seen the observed data configuration, or one considered more “extreme”. There is a subtlety here,

a large pµ value would indicate a high degree of compatibility between the signal hypothesis and the

data, however, it would not particularly favor a signal hypothesis over another, or, even the signal

hypothesis over the background hypothesis. Indeed, exceedingly small signal hypothesis would have

large pµ values whenever the observed data resembled the background. Instead, pµ is by construction

useful for exclusion. Whenever the observed data, and any data configuration considered more ex-

treme, is deemed to have only a 5% probability of occurring, the signal hypothesis is excluded at the

95% confidence level.

This treatment has an undesired property: exclusion limits can be set for diminishingly small signal

hypotheses. Naturally, physics analyses do not claim sensitivity to unobservable signal hypotheses. To

address this, the CLs method is used instead [112]. This entails modulating the signal p-value pµ,

dividing it by 1 −pb (also called CLb).

*Figure 10.5e presents the combined CLs grid when leveraging all four signal regions. The com-*

bined grid is the ultimate deliverable for the model-dependent interpretation and benchmarks the

BSM reach of the analysis as a whole.

The derived CLs values were then used to extrapolate a 95% confidence level exclusion contour,

shown in figure 10.6. This figure also shows the expected exclusion contour based on background

Asimov data [109], as well as the contours extrapolated from ±1σ CLs grids. The extrapolation

from a grid of CLs values to a contour is performed with a linear radial basis function interpolation.

However, this interpolation does not have a rigorous statistical basis. The more rigorous, and reinter-

pretable statistical result is encapsulated by the CLs values.

The observed exclusion contour is in good agreement with the expected exclusion contour – well

within the ±1σ envelope. For context, limits set on a scalar LQ from a previous pair production

ATLAS analysis are also plotted. These limits are independent of the Yukawa coupling, since the

signal LQs in that analysis were produced through the QCD interactions with gluons. Although the

presented resonant LQ production channel cannot compete with the pair production limits for low

couplings, the analysis offers competitive sensitivity for order one couplings, and improved sensitivity

for larger couplings.

## 11

## Outlook

The presented analysis probed the high energy frontier of muon and b-jet resonant final states by

studying nearly 200 fb−1 of collision data taken by ATLAS between 2015 and 2023. The observed

spectrumwasingoodagreementwiththenullhypothesis: theSMbackgroundprediction. Theresults

were benchmarked against the ˜S1 scalar LQ model, and demonstrated world-leading sensitivity to

such heavy resonances for Yukawa couplings above ∼1.

For couplings below ∼1, pair-production LQ searches are expected to beat resonant LQ searches

since pair production bypasses the cost of paying a Yukawa coupling. However, the signatures studied

in the pair-production searches are quite different. As a result, the presented resonant muon and b-

170


<!-- Page 190 -->


jet analysis is novel, and its reach in phase-space does not overlap with prior studies even for smaller

couplings.

Although purely signature-driven motivations for analyses at colliders are fraught with pitfalls –

most notably the look-elsewhere effect – SM particle resonances have played a powerful role in particle

physics discoveries. As such, particle resonances can be viewed as a privileged corner of phase-space.

Without going into details, there are roughly 9 clearly resolvable signatures by ATLAS: light-jets, c-

jets, b-jets, top quarks, the three charged leptons, neutrinos, and photons. This makes for roughly 92

possible flavor channel combinations (neglecting charge-conjugate channels) – many of which have

already been studied. Variations around this theme should be far removed from any look-elsewhere

effect limitations.

At this point in time when the naturalness-driven narrative of particle physics discoveries is being

questioned, taking partial steps back-ward to signature-driven motivations is a simple approach to

mappingoutavenuesforprobingthehighenergyfrontier. Heavyresonances,oralack-thereof,should

be a resolved feature of the picture of fundamental interactions below the 10−18 m length scale.
